breakfast.name: Khao Tom (Rice Soup)
instructions: Simmer stock with garlic and ginger
Add leftover rice — it breaks down into a soft, porridge-like soup
Season with fish sauce and lime juice
Serve topped with scallions, cilantro, crispy shallots
The rice half-dissolves, thickening the broth
Optional: float a soft-boiled egg on top
Khao Tom is Laos's everyday breakfast — light, easy to digest
The crispy shallot topping provides the textural contrast
Every Lao household has leftover rice — khao tom is the solution
Simple but deeply satisfying as a morning reset
breakfast.description: Laos's everyday breakfast rice soup — leftover rice simmered in pork broth until softened, topped with crispy shallots, cilantro, and lime. Light and restorative, it's the morning reset dish of Lao households. The crispy shallot crunch against the soft rice is the textural key.

breakfast.name: Khao Niaow (Sticky Rice with Sides)
instructions: Soak glutinous rice overnight — this is non-negotiable
Steam in a bamboo conical basket for 20-25 minutes
The rice cooks purely from steam — no water contact
The grains stick together but each is distinct — not gluey
Wet hands, roll into balls by hand — the traditional way to eat
Dip into nam prik or use to scoop up grilled meat or fish
Sticky rice is Laos's soul food — eaten three meals a day
The bamboo conical basket (huad) is Lao's most distinctive kitchen tool
Lao people eat more sticky rice per capita than anyone on earth
The ritual of rolling balls by hand connects to every meal, every memory
breakfast.description: Laos's soul food — glutinous rice steamed in the iconic bamboo conical basket (huad), eaten by hand in rolled balls at every meal. Lao people consume more sticky rice per capita than any nation. The overnight soak, the steam-only cooking method, and the hand-rolling ritual are central to Lao identity.

breakfast.name: Patongko (Lao Fried Dough)
ingredients: Sweetened condensed milk or pandan jam for dipping
instructions: Mix flour, baking powder, salt, sugar with water into a soft dough
Rest 15 minutes
Pull into elongated sticks, double them up — the classic shape is two pieces joined
Deep fry at 175°C until puffed and golden
The baking powder gives them a gentle hollow interior
Serve immediately — they deflate slightly as they cool
Dip into condensed milk or pandan jam
Patongko is the Lao-Chinese morning snack — sold at every morning market
The golden puffed sticks with condensed milk is the Lao breakfast image
Street vendors fry them fresh from 5am — the oil smell wakes up the market
breakfast.description: Laos's Chinese-influenced breakfast sticks — doubled dough sticks deep-fried until hollow and golden, dipped in sweetened condensed milk. Sold at every morning market from 5am. The street-corner frying smell and the condensed milk dip are quintessentially Lao-Chinese morning culture.

breakfast.name: Khao Piak Sen (Rice Noodle Soup)
ingredients: Bean sprouts, herbs: cilantro, sawtooth herb
instructions: Build a clear broth with pork/chicken bones, ginger, shallots — simmer 1 hour
Strain to a clear, golden broth
Prepare fresh rice noodles — thick and silky, not dried
Blanch noodles briefly in boiling water
Build the bowl: noodles, thin-sliced pork or chicken, ladle of hot broth
Top with bean sprouts, herbs, crispy garlic oil, chili
Squeeze lime at the table
Khao piak sen is Laos's answer to Vietnamese pho — gentler, less complex but deeply homey
The fresh thick rice noodles are uniquely Lao — silkier than dried
The crispy garlic oil is Laos's universal flavor brightener
breakfast.description: Laos's homey noodle soup — fresh thick rice noodles in clear pork or chicken broth, topped with crispy garlic oil, herbs, and lime. Softer and less structured than Vietnamese pho, it's more about comfort than complexity. The crispy garlic oil is the distinctly Lao finishing touch.

lunch.name: Larb (Minced Meat Salad)
ingredients: Minced pork, chicken, or beef (or raw/rare — larb dip)
instructions: Toast dry rice in a dry pan until golden brown — grind into coarse powder
This toasted rice powder is the defining texture of larb — smoky, nutty, grainy
Cook minced meat in a dry hot pan with minimal water — keep it coarse
Dress while still warm with lime juice, fish sauce, chili flakes, shallots
Add toasted rice powder — it absorbs the dressing and adds texture
Toss with fresh herbs: mint, cilantro, sawtooth herb
Serve with sticky rice and raw vegetable sides
Larb is considered Laos's national dish — it IS Lao cuisine to many
The toasted rice powder distinguishes larb from all other Southeast Asian salads
Larb traveled to Thailand as laap but the Lao version is the original
lunch.description: Laos's national dish — minced meat dressed in lime, fish sauce, chili, and the defining toasted rice powder (khao khua). The smoky, nutty rice powder that soaks up the dressing is uniquely Lao. Larb traveled to Thailand as laap, but the Lao version — with raw galangal and abundant mint — is the original.

lunch.name: Tam Mak Houng (Lao Papaya Salad)
ingredients: Padek (fermented fish paste — the Lao distinction)
instructions: Pound garlic and chilies in a mortar — the number of chilies is the heat gauge
Add long beans, pound lightly
Add shredded papaya, tomatoes, dried shrimp
Add padek (fermented fish paste) — this is what separates Lao papaya salad from Thai
Dress with lime juice, fish sauce, palm sugar — pound and toss
Finish with crushed peanuts
Taste: it should be simultaneously spicy, sour, salty, slightly sweet
The padek (fermented fish paste) makes Lao papaya salad funkier and deeper than Thai som tam
This is the most-eaten dish in Laos — consumed daily at every meal
The pounding is a workout — Lao cooks can hear whether it's ready
lunch.description: Laos's most-eaten dish — shredded green papaya pounded in a mortar with bird's eye chili, garlic, tomatoes, and padek (fermented fish paste). The padek makes it funkier, deeper, and more complex than Thai som tam. The pounding rhythm, the multiple chili heat, and the five-way flavor balance (spicy/sour/salty/sweet/funky) are Lao hallmarks.

lunch.name: Khao Poon (Noodle Curry Soup)
ingredients: Red curry paste or galangal-lemongrass paste
Fresh vegetables: banana blossom, bean sprouts, long beans
instructions: Build the curry base: fry curry paste in oil until fragrant
Add coconut milk, lemongrass, kaffir lime — simmer
Add protein — pork shoulder works well, simmer until tender
Season with fish sauce, lime
Prepare rice vermicelli — soak in water until soft, blanch
Serve as a build-your-own bowl: noodles at the bottom
Pour curry broth over, top with banana blossom, bean sprouts
Finish with fresh herbs, extra lime
Khao poon is Laos's festive noodle soup — served at every ceremony and celebration
The coconut-lemongrass broth is Southeast Asian in base but distinctly Lao in assembly
lunch.description: Laos's festive noodle soup — rice vermicelli in coconut curry broth, assembled at the table with banana blossom, bean sprouts, and fresh herbs. Served at every Lao ceremony and celebration. The self-assembly ritual and the lemongrass-coconut broth with Lao fresh herb variety make it distinct from Thai curries.

lunch.name: Or Lam (Lao Forest Stew)
ingredients: Sakhan (wood vine — the signature Lao spice, very aromatic)
instructions: Sakhan (krai or sakhaan) is the key ingredient — a wild vine with a peppery, warming flavor
Without sakhan, or lam is not authentic — it's the defining flavor
Brown pork or smoked pork in a clay pot
Add water, bring to a simmer
Add sakhan, lemongrass, galangal, kaffir lime — the forest aromatic base
Add eggplant, long beans, mushrooms
Simmer slowly 30-40 minutes — the stew should be thick, concentrated
Season with fish sauce, dried chili
Or lam is the ancient food of Luang Prabang — the old royal capital's stew
The use of sakhan vine is uniquely Lao — found wild in forest, not cultivated
lunch.description: Luang Prabang's ancient royal stew — pork with sakhan vine (a wild Lao forest spice), eggplant, and long beans. Sakhan is the defining ingredient: peppery, aromatic, found wild in forests and unsubstitutable. This stew from the old royal capital carries the flavor of Lao highland forest.

dinner.name: Mok Pa (Steamed Fish in Banana Leaf)
ingredients: Red curry paste or kroeung paste
Dill (yes — Lao cuisine uses dill, unusual in SE Asia)
instructions: Make the paste: blend galangal, lemongrass, kaffir lime, chili — or use red curry paste
Mix fish with paste, coconut milk, egg, dill — the dill is Lao's unique flavor signature
Dill is rarely used in other SE Asian cuisines — its presence marks Lao cooking distinctly
Spoon onto banana leaf squares, fold into parcels
Tie with banana leaf strips or toothpicks
Steam 25-30 minutes — the banana leaf imparts a subtle green vegetable aroma
The fish custard sets inside the leaf — it should be springy, not watery
Unwrap at the table — the steam and fragrance are part of the experience
Mok pa represents Lao's most distinctive cooking style — steaming in banana leaf
The dill-coconut-fish combination is completely unique to Laos
dinner.description: Laos's most distinctive dish — fish custard steamed in banana leaf with dill (uniquely Lao — almost no other Southeast Asian cuisine uses dill), coconut milk, and forest aromatics. The banana leaf steaming, the dill fragrance, and the custardy fish texture inside the parcel are the hallmarks of Lao cooking.

dinner.name: Ping Gai (Lao Grilled Chicken)
ingredients: Marinade: lemongrass, galangal, garlic, coriander root
instructions: Pound marinade ingredients into a paste: lemongrass, galangal, garlic, coriander root
Turmeric gives the chicken its golden color when grilled
Marinate chicken 2+ hours or overnight
Grill over charcoal — the charcoal smoke is essential
Flatten the chicken to grill evenly — a Lao technique is pressing it with a weight
The skin should be charred and golden, the meat juicy
Serve with sticky rice and jeow bong (a cooked chili relish)
Ping gai stands outside every Lao restaurant — the charcoal grill is the sign you've arrived
The smoke, the golden turmeric skin, and the jeow bong dip are Lao charcoal cooking at its best
Almost every evening meal in Laos includes grilled meat over charcoal
dinner.description: Laos's charcoal grill icon — turmeric-golden chicken marinated in lemongrass and galangal paste, grilled over charcoal until the skin chars and the meat stays juicy. Served with sticky rice and jeow bong chili relish. The charcoal smoke, the turmeric color, and the dipping relish are the Lao grilled meat experience.

dinner.name: Naem Khao (Crispy Rice Salad)
ingredients: Naem (fermented pork sausage — the key ingredient)
instructions: Mix day-old rice with red curry paste, shredded coconut, egg — form into balls
Deep fry the rice balls until shatteringly crispy on the outside
The fried rice balls crumble when tossed — creating crispy shards
Toss crispy rice with naem (fermented pork), peanuts, dried shrimp, herbs
Dress with lime juice and fish sauce
The naem is the sour, funky key — Lao fermented pork sausage
The dish is assembled to order — the crunch is the moment
Naem khao is a Vientiane street food classic and the most photogenic Lao dish
The golden crispy rice shards with fresh herbs and fermented pork are visually striking
Wrap in lettuce for a refreshing, contrasting bite
dinner.description: Vientiane's street food icon — deep-fried rice balls crumbled into shards and tossed with fermented pork (naem), herbs, peanuts, and lime. The crispy rice shards and the fermented pork tang are uniquely Lao. The golden, herb-scattered salad is the most photogenic Lao dish and a must-order in the capital.

dinner.name: Kaipen (Fried River Weed)
ingredients: Kaipen (dried Mekong river weed / algae — the Lao delicacy)
instructions: Kaipen is harvested from the Mekong River — seasonal, precious
It is dried in large flat sheets on bamboo frames in the sun
The dried sheets smell of river and seaweed
Fry briefly in oil — it puffs and crisps instantly
Sprinkle with sesame seeds while hot
The texture becomes like a crispy chip — light, slightly salty, intensely umami
Dip into jeow bong (a roasted chili relish with tomatoes)
Kaipen is only available in northern Laos — a Mekong River delicacy
It represents Laos's intimate relationship with the Mekong River
The seasonal harvest, the Mekong source, and the unique texture make kaipen culturally irreplaceable
dinner.description: The Mekong River snack — dried river algae (kaipen) fried until crispy like chips, sprinkled with sesame seeds. Harvested seasonally from the Mekong and sun-dried on bamboo frames. Only available in northern Laos. The Mekong River source, the seasonal scarcity, and the intensely umami crispy texture make kaipen one of Southeast Asia's most unusual foods.

snacks.name: Khao Jee (Grilled Sticky Rice Cakes)
instructions: Shape leftover sticky rice into flat oval patties
Brush with beaten egg on both sides
Sprinkle sesame seeds
Grill over charcoal or in a pan — the egg creates a golden, slightly crispy shell
The interior stays soft and warm from the sticky rice
The egg creates a savory film around the rice cake
Eat as a snack, with jeow, or as a side
Khao jee (or grilled rice cakes) is the Lao solution to leftover sticky rice
The charcoal-grilled version has a smoky edge that the pan version lacks
Sold by street vendors near morning markets
snacks.description: Laos's leftover sticky rice snack — rice shaped into patties, egg-brushed, and grilled over charcoal until the exterior crisps. The egg creates a golden film; the interior stays soft. A morning market street food and the elegant Lao solution to yesterday's sticky rice.

snacks.name: Sai Oua (Lao Herb Sausage)
instructions: Grind/mince pork with all aromatics — lemongrass, galangal, garlic, dill
The dill-kaffir lime combination is distinctly Lao
Stuff into pork casing or form into long patties
Grill over charcoal — the fat renders, the aromatics bloom
The outside should be deeply golden, slightly charred
The interior stays juicy and aromatic
The dill and kaffir lime are the scent signature — you can smell sai oua before you see it
Sai oua is Luang Prabang's most famous sausage — a UNESCO city's specialty
The herbal fragrance and the snap of the casing are the textural hooks
Served with sticky rice and a cold Beer Lao
snacks.description: Luang Prabang's herbal pork sausage — ground fatty pork packed with lemongrass, galangal, dill, and kaffir lime zest, grilled over charcoal. The dill-kaffir lime fragrance is distinctly Lao and announces the sausage before you see it. A specialty of the UNESCO heritage city, served with sticky rice.

snacks.name: Sin Dat (Lao Table BBQ)
ingredients: Lard or pork fat (for the dome)
Dipping broth: pork bones, lemongrass, galangal
instructions: Sin dat is a clay pot with a domed lid — fat greases the dome while vegetables simmer in the moat
Heat the dome with lard so it glistens
Grill meat on the dome — the fat-basted surface is the key flavor
Vegetables and broth cook in the moat surrounding the dome
The dome gives a slightly caramelized, fatty char to the meat
Build your own bite: dome-grilled meat + broth-cooked veg + nam jim
Sin dat is Laos's table grill — like Korean BBQ or Japanese shabu, but distinctly Lao
The clay domed pot is the cooking vessel and the cultural artifact
Evening sin dat with friends and Beer Lao is the Lao social meal
The dome-moat concept is unique to Laos and northeast Thailand
snacks.description: Laos's table grill — a clay domed pot where fat-greased dome grills meat while vegetables simmer in the surrounding moat broth. Build your own bite combining dome-grilled meat, broth-softened vegetables, and chili-lime dipping sauce. Like Korean BBQ but distinctly Lao, the sin dat clay pot is both cooking vessel and cultural artifact.

snacks.name: Jeow Bong (Lao Chili Relish)
instructions: Roast whole shallots and garlic in their skins directly in the fire or on a dry pan
Char them — the charred skin is removed, the smoky flesh used
Roast dried chilies until fragrant
Pound everything in a mortar: chilies, galangal, garlic, shallot
Add padek and palm sugar — the fermented fish makes it deep and funky
Adjust seasoning: it should be smoky, spicy, sweet, salty, funky in balance
Toast sesame seeds, stir in
Jeow bong is Laos's condiment soul — it goes with everything
It appears on every Lao table, made in every household
The charred roasted flavors and padek depth are the Lao relish signature
snacks.description: Laos's essential table condiment — a smoky, spicy, funky relish of roasted chilies, charred shallots, and galangal pounded with fermented fish paste. Appears on every Lao table with every meal. The charred-roasted depth and the padek funk are the flavor signatures that make Lao food unmistakably Lao.

snacks.name: Ping Pa (Grilled Fish on Bamboo)
ingredients: Bamboo sticks for grilling over charcoal
instructions: Stuff fish cavity with lemongrass, galangal, chili, salt
Secure with banana leaf strips or tie with bamboo
Skewer through head and tail with long bamboo stakes
Grill over charcoal at an angle
The fish cooks slowly — 15-20 min per side
The lemongrass inside perfumes the flesh from inside out
The skin chars and crisps — peel away at the table
The white fish beneath is fragrant with galangal and smoke
River fish is central to Lao cuisine — the Mekong provides most protein
The bamboo-staked whole fish at the riverside grill is the most Lao image in existence
snacks.description: The most iconic Lao image — whole river fish stuffed with lemongrass and galangal, staked on bamboo and grilled over charcoal at the riverside. The Mekong River provides most of Laos's protein and bamboo fishing-grilling culture is the country's culinary identity. The fragrant lemongrass-smoke infusion and the char-and-peel at the table are the ritual.

desserts.name: Khao Tom (Sweet Sticky Rice in Banana Leaf)
ingredients: Pandan leaf (for color and fragrance — optional)
instructions: Mix soaked glutinous rice with coconut milk and palm sugar
Add pandan leaf juice for green color (optional)
Place rice on banana leaf square, add filling (black bean or banana)
Fold banana leaf into a tight rectangular parcel
Tie with banana leaf strips — the tying technique varies by region
Steam 25-30 minutes
The banana leaf imparts a subtle grassy sweetness to the rice
The rice becomes a dense, sweet, fragrant block
Khao tom is Laos's everyday sweet — offered at temples, sold at markets
The banana-leaf parcel unwrapping is an ancient ritual of anticipation
desserts.description: Laos's temple sweet — glutinous rice with coconut milk and palm sugar steamed in banana leaf into a dense, fragrant block. Offered at Buddhist temples and sold at every market. The banana leaf imparts a green, grassy sweetness. Unwrapping the parcel is a small ritual of anticipation repeated at every ceremony.

desserts.name: Khao Niaow Ma Muang (Mango Sticky Rice)
instructions: Steam glutinous rice in bamboo basket
Mix warm coconut milk with palm sugar and salt
Pour half the coconut milk over hot sticky rice — let it absorb
The rice should be creamy, not wet
Slice ripe mango alongside
Drizzle remaining coconut milk over the assembled plate
Scatter toasted sesame seeds
The sweet-salt coconut milk dressing is the secret — the salt makes it luxurious
Mango sticky rice is shared across Laos and Thailand but the Lao version uses more coconut
The ripe mango must be fragrant — an unripe mango ruins the dish
This is Laos's most universally beloved sweet — the tropical luxury dessert
desserts.description: Southeast Asia's luxury dessert — steamed sticky rice drenched in salted-sweet coconut milk with sliced ripe mango. The salt in the coconut milk is the secret that makes the whole dish luxurious. Shared across Laos and Thailand, the Lao version uses richer, more coconut-forward dressing.

desserts.name: Nam Van Saku (Tapioca Coconut Pudding)
ingredients: Taro, sweet potato, or corn (optional additions)
instructions: Soak tapioca pearls 30 minutes
Simmer in water until translucent — the centers turn completely clear
Add coconut milk, palm sugar, pandan leaves — simmer gently
The pandan turns the coconut milk a pale green — and gives a floral fragrance
Add cooked taro or sweet potato if desired
Serve warm or with shaved ice
The translucent tapioca pearls in pale green coconut milk are visually beautiful
Nam van saku is Laos's refreshing temple dessert — served at ceremonies
The pandan-coconut fragrance is the scent of Lao dessert culture
The chewy-smooth tapioca in warm coconut milk is deeply comforting
desserts.description: Laos's temple pudding — translucent tapioca pearls in pandan-fragrant coconut milk, served warm or over ice. The pale green pandan tint and the warm coconut milk fragrance are the sensory identity of Lao dessert culture. Served at Buddhist ceremonies and found at every market sweet stall.

desserts.name: Sangkhaya (Coconut Custard)
ingredients: Young coconut shell or pumpkin (as container)
instructions: Crack eggs, beat gently — no over-beating (creates bubbles)
Mix with coconut milk, palm sugar, pandan juice
Pour into a young coconut shell or hollowed-out pumpkin
Steam gently — 40-45 minutes
The custard should be just set — it jiggles slightly in the center
It sets more as it cools — remove from steamer at just-set stage
The coconut shell or pumpkin shell is the traditional serving vessel
The custard takes on the faint coconut flavor of the shell
Sangkhaya is Laos's royal dessert — also common in Thailand and Cambodia
The custard surface should be perfectly smooth and quivering
desserts.description: Laos's royal coconut custard — eggs, coconut milk, and palm sugar steamed in a young coconut shell until just set. The coconut shell is both the cooking vessel and the serving dish, lending its faint sweetness to the custard. A royal-origin dessert shared across mainland Southeast Asia.

drinks.name: Lao Lao (Lao Rice Whisky)
ingredients: Luk Paeng (yeast balls — traditional fermentation starter)
Still or recycled bottles for storage
instructions: Mix cooked sticky rice with luk paeng yeast balls
Ferment in a sealed container 3-5 days at room temperature
The rice converts to a milky, sweet mash
Distill — traditional home distillation using simple clay pot stills
The first distillate is the strongest — high proof
Lao Lao is typically 40-45% ABV, clear
Serve neat in small glasses — drinking is communal and ritualistic
Lao Lao is consumed at every village ceremony, wedding, and spirit ceremony
Home distillation is legal and common in Laos — every village makes it
The quality varies wildly — from harsh to surprisingly smooth
drinks.description: Laos's moonshine — home-distilled sticky rice whisky made with traditional yeast balls, drunk neat at every village ceremony and celebration. Home distillation is legal in Laos, making every village a producer. The communal, ritualistic drinking and the variable quality (from harsh to smooth) are the Lao Lao experience.

drinks.name: Beer Lao
ingredients: Ice (Lao beer is always drunk over ice — the climate demands it)
instructions: Pour Beer Lao over a glass full of ice
The ice dilutes it slightly but the tropical heat demands cold
Beer Lao is the most popular beer in Southeast Asia by enthusiast rankings
It's made from jasmine rice — which gives it a subtle sweetness
The jasmine rice gives it a character unlike European lagers
Drink with grilled chicken (ping gai), sin dat, or a plate of sai oua
Beer Lao with grilled food is the Lao evening
The brand identity — the brown bottle, the golden label — is everywhere in Laos
Beer Lao is a source of national pride — a Lao product that's globally recognized
Sip over ice and watch the Mekong — the optimal serving condition
drinks.description: Laos's liquid pride — jasmine-rice lager brewed locally, always drunk over ice in the tropical heat. The jasmine rice gives Beer Lao a subtle sweetness that distinguishes it from European lagers. The most praised beer in Southeast Asia, it's a rare Lao consumer product with genuine global recognition.

drinks.name: Nam Ma Kham (Tamarind Juice)
instructions: Soak tamarind pods or paste in warm water — 15 minutes
Work the tamarind flesh apart with your hands — it dissolves into the water
Strain through a sieve — pushing to extract all the pulp
The liquid is thick, deep brown, intensely sour
Sweeten with palm sugar to taste — the palm sugar's caramel note suits tamarind
Add a pinch of salt — the salt sharpens the sourness beautifully
Serve over ice
Nam ma kham is Laos's most refreshing street drink
The sour-sweet balance is more intense than other tropical drinks
The tamarind's deep sour note and the palm sugar caramel hit together are perfect
drinks.description: Laos's street refresher — tamarind dissolved in water, balanced with palm sugar and a pinch of salt, served over ice. The sour-sweet contrast is more intense than any other tropical drink and the palm sugar caramel note against tamarind's deep acidity is a perfect pairing. A daily market drink across Southeast Asia.

drinks.name: Lao Coffee (Café Lao)
ingredients: Lao ground coffee (Bolaven Plateau — grown at altitude)
instructions: Brew Lao coffee through a traditional cloth sock-filter or drip method
Lao coffee from the Bolaven Plateau is medium-roast, earthy, and full-bodied
Add a generous pour of sweetened condensed milk to the glass
Pour hot coffee over — the condensed milk swirls up through it
Stir or leave layered
Serve over ice for iced version — the most popular way
The condensed milk sweetness against the earthy, bold Lao coffee is perfect
The Bolaven Plateau produces some of Southeast Asia's best arabica and robusta
Lao coffee is a UNESCO-recognized craft product
The coffee sock-filter is the traditional Southeast Asian brewing method — portable, cheap, perfect
drinks.description: Coffee from the clouds — Lao Bolaven Plateau arabica brewed through a cloth sock-filter, poured over condensed milk and ice. The Bolaven Plateau (1,300m elevation) produces some of Southeast Asia's most acclaimed coffee. The cloth-sock brewing tradition and the condensed milk sweetness against earthy coffee are the Lao café ritual.
